1401.title: Bringing it home
1401.hook: all the year's learning into one day's shape
1401.howItsDone: Muslims shape the day around the daily prayers, from dawn to night, and fill the time between with work, family and small acts of worship such as remembrance of Allah, reading the Qur'an and giving.

segments.voice: Yesterday: art and music debates, two girls singing on Eid and a flute of the family of David. Your line was views differ, voices rise. The questions of today are done; now, a practice for today.

A river runs past your front door. That's the picture the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, gives his companions in Sahih al-Bukhari. Suppose, he says, in paraphrase, there were a river at someone's door, and he bathed in it five times a day. Would any dirt be left on him? None at all, they say. That, he says, is the five prayers: through them Allah wipes away wrongs. Not one great washing a year. A river, at the door, every day.
screen: `A RIVER AT THE DOOR.` → `FIVE TIMES A DAY.` → `A RIVER, EVERY DAY.`

segments.voice: Start where the day starts, with intention. The first report in Sahih al-Bukhari says, in paraphrase, that actions are judged by their intentions, and each person gets what they intended. So a day begins before the alarm is off: what is today for? Then the frame. The Qur'an gives it in the chapter called Hud, in Pickthall's translation: "Establish worship at the two ends of the day and in some watches of the night. Lo! good deeds annul ill deeds." The two ends of the day: dawn and dusk, with prayers in between, so that work, school, errands and meals all happen inside a frame, the way a river runs between its banks. Inside that frame go the small things this path has been collecting: the bismillah before eating, the greeting of peace, a word kept kind, a debt remembered, a coin set aside, a minute of Qur'an. None of them is large. That's the point of the last piece. Al-Bukhari keeps a saying, reported by 'Aisha, that the deeds most loved by Allah are the ones done regularly, even if they are small. Not the heroic weekend. The steady weekday. So the shape of a whole day, in this tradition, is not a schedule of impressive acts. It's an intention at the start, a frame of prayer, small good deeds in the gaps, and a return to the river, again and again. What comes home from a year of learning, in this picture, is not a pile of facts. It's a day with a shape.
screen: `FIRST, THE INTENTION.` · `THE TWO ENDS OF THE DAY.` · `SMALL GOOD THINGS IN THE GAPS.` · `REGULAR, EVEN IF SMALL.` · then, large: `A RIVER AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Picture waking up tomorrow and the first thing you'd like to intend, then move through the day in your mind, placing one small thing at each part: a prayer if you pray, a breath, a kind word, a moment of thanks, a few verses read. Keep each one small enough to really do. Then picture lying down at night, the day done, the frame held.
Bringing it home. Gathering a year's learning into one day's shape: an intention, the frame of prayer, small good deeds done regularly. Today's word.
Your line: a day, whole. Small, regular, and held in a frame. See you tomorrow.

1402.title: Your school
1402.hook: knowing which school you follow, or finding one
1402.howItsDone: A Muslim may follow one school of law, a madhhab such as the Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali or Ja'fari, often learned through family or a teacher, and look up its rulings for everyday questions of prayer, fasting and purity; some prefer to weigh the evidence without binding themselves to one school.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bringing it home, a river at the door, and one ordinary day given a shape. Your line was a day, whole.

Two friends stand shoulder to shoulder in a prayer row. When the imam begins, one folds her hands on her chest. The woman beside her lets her arms hang straight at her sides. Afterward a newcomer asks which of them did it wrong. They both laugh. Neither, they say: each learned it from her school. You met this back on day one hundred ten. A school here is not a building. It's a madhhab, a way of reading the Qur'an and the Sunnah that scholars worked through, question by question, and handed on.
screen: `TWO WAYS TO STAND, ONE ROW.` → `NEITHER IS WRONG.` → `A SCHOOL IS NOT A BUILDING.`

segments.voice: In a story in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, sent his companions out and told them not to pray the afternoon prayer until they reached a certain place. On the road, the time began to run out. Some said: he meant hurry, so we pray now. Others said: he said there, so we wait. They did both, and when they told him, he blamed neither group. Faithful people, reading the same words, can reach different conclusions in good faith. Among Sunni Muslims the well-known schools are the Hanafi, the Maliki, the Shafi'i and the Hanbali, each named for a teacher: Abu Hanifa, Malik ibn Anas, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad ibn Hanbal. Twelver Shia Muslims follow the Ja'fari school, named for Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq, and Ibadi Muslims keep their own. Some follow the school of their family or region, the way you inherit a recipe. Some choose one through a teacher. In Twelver Shia practice, a believer who isn't a scholar follows a living senior scholar for rulings. And some Muslims, including some Salafis, prefer not to tie themselves to one school and look at the evidence directly, while others answer that a school is the safer road for anyone who isn't a scholar. Each side makes its case from the Qur'an and the Sunnah. On a Tuesday, a school answers small questions. What breaks your wudu. How a traveler shortens prayers. What to do if you forget a step. The Qur'an tells people who don't know to ask those who do. A school is one way of knowing whom to ask.
screen: `TWO READINGS, NEITHER BLAMED.` · `THE SCHOOLS AND THEIR TEACHERS.` · `INHERIT, CHOOSE, OR LOOK DIRECTLY.` · `SMALL QUESTIONS, REAL ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one act of worship you do, or have watched someone do, like washing before prayer, and walk through it slowly, step by step. At each step, ask: do I know why it's done this way, or only that it is? Where you're unsure, stop; if you pray, set the intention to learn that one step properly, and if you don't, just stay with the question.
Your school. A madhhab, a tested way of reading the Qur'an and the Sunnah, named for a teacher and handed down. Today's word.
Your line: know your school. Every small answer you live by comes from somewhere. Until tomorrow.

1403.title: Your teacher
1403.hook: the value of a living teacher
1403.howItsDone: Muslims study with teachers in mosques, schools and homes, especially for the Qur'an, which is learned by reciting aloud to a teacher who corrects the pronunciation; some students look for a teacher whose own learning comes through a chain of teachers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: your school, the companions on the road, and a madhhab as one way of knowing whom to ask. Your line was know your school.

The companions are sitting with the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, when a stranger walks in. His clothes are bright white, his hair very black, and there's no dust of travel on him. Nobody knows him. He sits so close that his knees touch the Prophet's knees, rests his hands on his thighs, and starts asking. What is Islam? What is faith? What is excellence? After he leaves, the Prophet tells them who it was: Jibril, who came to teach you your religion. That's how Sahih Muslim tells it. Knee to knee.
screen: `A STRANGER WITH NO DUST ON HIM.` → `KNEE TO KNEE.` → `HE CAME TO TEACH YOU.`

segments.voice: Jibril could have left a scroll. Instead, the religion was taught as a conversation between two people sitting close, with questions, answers, and witnesses who carried it on. The Qur'an travels the same way. It's a recitation, heard and repeated. A student sits with a teacher who listens and corrects a vowel, a pause, a letter held too short. In Sahih al-Bukhari the Prophet says the best of you are those who learn the Qur'an and teach it: learning and teaching in the same sentence. Even a prophet went looking for a teacher. In surah al-Kahf, Musa travels to find a servant of God who has been given knowledge, and asks to follow him so that he may be taught. The man warns him he won't have the patience. What follows is a lesson in exactly that: a student who keeps interrupting, and a teacher who bears with him twice before they part. So a teacher isn't only someone who knows more. A teacher can see you, your mistakes, your rushing, your gaps, and say so kindly. People find one today in many ways. Some study with an imam at a local mosque. Some join a class for women taught by a woman scholar. Some begin online and then look for a person they can sit with. Musa's own words are a good model for the asking: may I follow you, so that you teach me? A request, not a demand.
screen: `A LESSON GIVEN KNEE TO KNEE.` · `A RECITATION, HEARD AND CORRECTED.` · `MUSA GOES LOOKING FOR A TEACHER.` · `A TEACHER CAN SEE YOU.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you've tried to learn alone and stalled on: a surah you keep stumbling through, a question you keep meaning to settle, a skill half-learned from videos. Picture asking someone for help with it, face to face, the way Musa asked, and quietly name what makes the asking hard, pride, shyness, not knowing whom to ask, without obeying it. If you pray, ask Allah to make the asking easier.
Your teacher. A living person who learned from someone, and can sit close enough to correct you. Today's word.
Your line: find a teacher. Some things are only learned knee to knee. I'll be here tomorrow.

1404.title: Your mosque
1404.howItsDone: On Friday around midday, Muslims gather at the mosque for Jumu'ah: a sermon from the imam followed by a congregational prayer, which is required of adult resident men and open to women, and which takes the place of the noon prayer for those who attend.

segments.voice: Yesterday: your teacher, Jibril knee to knee, and Musa asking to follow. Your line was find a teacher.

Friday, a little after noon. Outside a door, shoes pile up in crooked rows: work boots, sneakers, a toddler's sandals, polished office shoes. Inside, a man who fixes cars stands next to a man who teaches at the university, and neither one is thinking about that. A taxi driver slips into the back row. Somebody's grandmother is already in her usual spot. For a few minutes, nobody is anyone's boss. Then the row straightens, and they bow together. Day one hundred thirty-seven asked what a mosque is. Today, what it's like to belong to one.
screen: `SHOES IN CROOKED ROWS.` → `NOBODY IS ANYONE'S BOSS.` → `THE ROW STRAIGHTENS.`

segments.voice: Start with the call. Surah al-Jumu'ah says, in Pickthall's words: "O ye who believe! When the call is heard for the prayer of the day of congregation, haste unto remembrance of Allah and leave your trading." In the Sunni schools of law the Friday prayer, with its sermon, is required of adult men who are settled in a place, and women may attend; when they do, it takes the place of the noon prayer. Why together? In Sahih al-Bukhari the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says prayer in congregation is twenty-seven degrees better than prayer alone. Twenty-seven is the hadith's own number. The point underneath is simple: the same prayer, said shoulder to shoulder, isn't the same experience. Who gets to come? In another hadith in Bukhari, the Prophet says not to stop the women servants of Allah from the mosques of Allah. Mosques today arrange space for women in different ways, and Muslims discuss openly how well that's working. And what belonging asks. A mosque isn't a perfect place. The sermon may run long; the parking may be a mess; someone may be rude about where you stood. Belonging isn't the same as liking everything. It means you're known by face, you notice when someone is missing, and somebody notices when you are. That's a lot to ask of a building, and it's exactly what people go back for.
screen: `THE CALL ON THE DAY OF CONGREGATION.` · `SHOULDER TO SHOULDER.` · `DON'T STOP THE WOMEN FROM THE MOSQUES.` · `BELONGING IS BEING MISSED.`

segments.voice: Think of a place where you're known by face, a mosque, a team, a building where someone waves, and let rise the name of someone who would notice if you didn't come, then the name of someone who has stopped turning up. If you pray, ask Allah to keep them well; if you don't, simply hold them in mind. If you're Muslim and able, you might plan to go this Friday a little early; if you aren't Muslim, some mosques welcome visitors.
Your mosque. The place where the row straightens on Friday, and where you are known, and missed. Today's word.
Your line: belong somewhere. Known by face, and missed on the Fridays you're gone. Until tomorrow.

1405.title: Your circle
1405.howItsDone: Muslims gather in a halaqah, a study circle, at a mosque or in a home, to read a passage of the Qur'an or a hadith together, often with a teacher or a trusted commentary, and to discuss what it asks of daily life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: your mosque, the row on Friday, and belonging as being missed. Your line was belong somewhere.

A Tuesday evening. A living room with the couch pushed back. A pot of tea going cold because everyone forgot it. A handful of people on cushions in a rough ring, one mushaf open to a single page, and a question nobody can quite answer: what does this verse actually ask of us on a weekday? Someone checks a commentary. Someone admits she always misread that line. A teenager asks the question the adults were too shy to ask. No microphone, no stage, no front row. Just a ring of knees. The halaqah.
screen: `A RING OF CUSHIONS AND COLD TEA.` → `ONE PAGE, ONE QUESTION.` → `NO STAGE, NO FRONT ROW.`

segments.voice: Halaqah means a circle, and it's what Muslims call a group that sits together to learn. A promise comes attached. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says that whenever people gather in one of the houses of Allah, reciting His Book and studying it among themselves, calm comes down on them, mercy covers them, angels surround them, and Allah mentions them to those who are with Him. Notice: not one person reading alone. People studying among themselves. Why a circle and not a lecture? In a circle everyone faces the middle. The quiet person can be seen. A question can come from anywhere. The Qur'an, in surah al-Ma'idah, says in Pickthall's words: "Help ye one another unto righteousness and pious duty." A circle is a practical way to help one another: you keep each other coming back, and you hear the parts of a verse you'd have skimmed. What keeps a circle honest? It can drift into everyone sharing opinions with nothing underneath. So a circle does well to keep one anchor: a teacher who visits, a trusted commentary, a book worked through page by page. And good manners: one person speaks at a time, nobody mocks a question, and anyone may say, I don't know. Saying it out loud, in front of friends, is part of learning together.
screen: `HALAQAH: A CIRCLE TO LEARN.` · `CALM, MERCY, AND ANGELS AROUND.` · `EVERYONE FACES THE MIDDLE.` · `AN ANCHOR, AND I DON'T KNOW.`

segments.voice: In your mind, draw a small ring and seat a few people you'd actually like to learn with, a friend, a cousin, a neighbor, not the most impressive ones but the ones who'd show up. Place one thing in the middle, a short surah, a single hadith, a chapter of a book, and notice how it feels to imagine not learning alone. If you pray, ask Allah in your own words to bless whatever circle you join.
Halaqah. A circle of people who sit facing one another to learn their faith together. Today's word.
Your line: learn together. Nobody in the ring has to know it all. That's today, done.

1406.title: Your charity
1406.howItsDone: Alongside the required zakat, Muslims give sadaqah, voluntary charity, in any amount and at any time; some set up a regular gift, weekly or monthly, following surah al-Baqarah's praise of those who give by night and by day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the halaqah, a ring of knees, and anyone free to say I don't know. Your line was learn together.

On a kitchen shelf, between the rice and the tea, sits an old jam jar with a strip of tape on it. Someone has written one word on the tape in marker: sadaqah. Every evening, whoever empties their pockets drops in the loose change. Nobody makes a speech about it. Once a month the jar is emptied and the money goes somewhere: a food bank, a neighbor's medical bill, a well. The jar isn't impressive. It's just always there, filling slowly. You met the word on day one hundred forty-nine. Today, making it regular.
screen: `A JAR BETWEEN THE RICE AND THE TEA.` → `LOOSE CHANGE, EVERY EVENING.` → `NOT IMPRESSIVE. ALWAYS THERE.`

segments.voice: First, two gifts. Zakat is the required one: a set share of wealth, owed by those who have enough, to the groups the Qur'an names. Sadaqah is the open one: voluntary, no minimum, given at any hour. Then the rhythm. Surah al-Baqarah praises those who spend their wealth by night and by day, in secret and in the open, and says their reward is with their Lord. Not one event, but a pattern running through the hours. That's the case for the jar: a small gift that keeps going shapes the giver in a way a single grand gesture may not. The size of it? Earlier in the same surah, the Qur'an compares money spent in Allah's way to a single grain that grows seven ears, with a hundred grains in each ear: something small put in the ground and multiplied. The same surah says giving openly is good, and giving quietly to the poor is better for you. So a regular, quiet gift has two things going for it at once. And what counts? In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says every good deed is a charity. Another hadith in Bukhari names some: a good word, helping someone onto their mount, removing something harmful from the road. Sadaqah is wider than money. A regular sadaqah can be a monthly transfer, a weekly visit, or a jar of coins. What matters is that it comes back around.
screen: `ZAKAT REQUIRED, SADAQAH OPEN.` · `BY NIGHT AND BY DAY.` · `ONE GRAIN, SEVEN EARS.` · `EVERY GOOD DEED IS A CHARITY.`

segments.voice: Let your hands rest open on your knees, palms up, and notice how little effort it takes to hold them open. Think of what you could give regularly without strain, a small amount each week, an hour of time, a meal for someone, small enough that you'd never skip it, and let one place it could go settle in your mind. If you pray, ask Allah to accept it.
Your charity. A regular sadaqah, small enough to keep, given again and again, quietly. Today's word.

1407.title: Your character
1407.hook: choosing one trait to work on for a year
1407.howItsDone: Muslims describe good character, akhlaq, as central to the faith, following the hadith that the best of people are those best in character; some choose one trait to work on, and practice muhasabah, a short daily self-accounting, to watch their progress.

segments.voice: Yesterday: your charity, a jar on the shelf, and sadaqah wider than money. Your line was regular giving.

"And lo! thou art of a tremendous nature." That's how Pickthall renders a line in surah al-Qalam, spoken to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. Of everything that could have been praised about him, his courage, his leadership, his patience in hard years, the verse praises his nature, his character. Someone once asked his wife Aisha what his character was like. Her answer, as Sahih Muslim records it: his character was the Qur'an. Not a summary of it. The Qur'an, walking around. Today, the hardest part of practice: choosing one trait to work on for a year.
screen: `A TREMENDOUS NATURE.` → `HIS CHARACTER WAS THE QUR'AN.` → `ONE TRAIT, ONE YEAR.`

segments.voice: In Sahih al-Bukhari the Prophet says the best of you are those with the best character. Of all the measures he could have picked, that's the one in this hadith. Now look at the week behind you. A school, a teacher, a mosque, a circle, a regular gift: none of these is the goal on its own. They're tools for becoming a certain kind of person. A ruling known by heart and a temper kept on a short leash are meant to belong to the same life. Why one trait? Character is slow work. Scholars of the inner life, such as al-Ghazali in his Revival of the Religious Sciences, describe treating a bad trait by practicing its opposite, deliberately, over and over, until the opposite starts to come naturally: the impatient person practicing waiting, the stingy one practicing giving. That's hard with ten traits at once. It's possible with one: patience, honesty, gentleness in speech, keeping promises, controlling anger. And the companion habit. The tradition calls it muhasabah, taking account of yourself. At the end of a day, a short honest look: where did my trait show up today, and where did it slip? No drama, no despair. Just a ledger, kept daily, the way you'd check a garden.
screen: `THE BEST IN CHARACTER.` · `THE WEEK'S TOOLS SERVE ONE GOAL.` · `PRACTICE THE OPPOSITE.` · `MUHASABAH: A DAILY LEDGER.`

segments.voice: Ask one honest question: which trait, if it grew in me this year, would make the people around me breathe easier? Not the one that sounds best; the one your family would choose for you. Let a word come, patience, gentleness, honesty, calm, then picture one moment this week where it was missing, without punishing yourself, and see the same moment with it present; if you pray, ask Allah for help with it in your own words.
Your character. Akhlaq, the habits of the heart that show in how you treat people, worked on one trait at a time. Today's word.
Your line: one trait. Practiced on purpose, checked each night, for a year. A week of building, done.
